title: Jesus and the apostles on foods
source_text: Ἰστέον μέντοι γε ὅτι, Ἰουδαίων οἰομένων νοεῖν τὸν Μωϋσέως νόμον καὶ τηρούντων ἐπὶ τῶν βρωμάτων τὸ μεταλαμβάνειν μὲν τῶν νενομισμένων αὐτοῖς καθαρῶν ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ τῶν ἀκαθάρτων ἀλλὰ καὶ μὴ χρῆσθαι αἵματι ζῴου εἰς τροφὴν μηδὲ τοῖς θηριαλώτοις καὶ ἄλλοις, περὶ ὧν πολὺς λόγος καὶ διὰ τοῦτο νῦν οὐκ εὔκαιρος ἐξετασθῆναι, ἡ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλία, βουλομένη πάντας ἀνθρώπους προσκαλέσασθαι εἰς τὴν καθαρὰν θεοσέβειαν καὶ μὴ προφάσει τῆς περὶ βρωμάτων βαρυτέρας νομοθεσίας κωλύειν πολλοὺς τῶν δυναμένων ὠφεληθῆναι εἰς ἤθη ἀπὸ χριστιανισμοῦ, ἀπεφήνατο ὅτι „οὐ τὰ εἰσερχόμενα εἰς τὸ στόμα κοινοὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐξερχόμενα ἐκ τοῦ στόματος“· τὰ μὲν γὰρ „εἰσερχόμενα εἰς τὸ στόμα εἰς τὴν κοιλίαν,“ φησὶ, „χωρεῖ καὶ εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται,“ τὰ δ᾿ ἐξιόντα ἐκ τοῦ στόματος „διαλογισμοί“ εἰσι „πονηροὶ“ λαλούμενοι καὶ „φόνοι“ καὶ „μοιχεῖαι“ καὶ „πορνεῖαι κλοπαί“ τε καὶ „ψευδομαρτυρίαι“ καὶ „βλασφημίαι.“ φησὶ δὲ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος ὅτι „βρῶμα ἡμᾶς οὐ παραστήσει τῷ θεῷ· οὔτε γὰρ ἐὰν φάγωμεν, περισσεύομεν, οὔτ᾿ ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα.“ εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ ἔχει τινὰ ἀσάφειαν ταῦτα, εἰ μὴ τύχῃ διαρθρώσεως, „ἔδοξε τοῖς τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀποστόλοις καὶ τοῖς“ ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ συναχθεῖσιν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ „πρεσβυτέροις“ καὶ, ὡς αὐτοὶ οὗτοι ὠνόμασαν, καὶ „τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι“ γράψαι τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν πιστεύουσιν ἐπιστολὴν, μόνα, ὡς ὠνόμασαν, „ἐπάναγκες“ ἀπαγορεύουσαν ἐσθίειν· ταῦτα δ᾿ ἐστὶ τὰ ητοι εἰδωλόθυτα ἢ τὰ πνικτὰ ἢ τὸ αἷμα.
pass_a_gloss: It must be known (ἰστέον), however, that, the Jews thinking (οἴομαι) to understand (νοέω) the law (νόμος) of Moses and keeping (τηρέω), with respect to foods (βρῶμα), the partaking (μεταλαμβάνω) of things held (νομίζω) by them clean (καθαρός) and abstaining from the unclean (ἀκάθαρτος), but also not using the blood (αἷμα) of an animal for nourishment (τροφή), nor things caught by beasts (θηριάλωτος), and others, about which [there is] much discourse (λόγος) and therefore not now timely (εὔκαιρος) to be examined, the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Jesus, wishing to call (προσκαλέομαι) all men to the pure worship of God and not by pretext (πρόφασις) of the heavier (βαρύς) legislation (νομοθεσία) about foods to hinder (κωλύω) many of those able to be benefited (ὠφελέω) in character (ἤθη) by Christianity (χριστιανισμός), declared (ἀποφαίνομαι) that 'not the things entering into the mouth defile (κοινόω) the man, but the things coming out of the mouth'; for the things 'entering into the mouth go into the belly (κοιλία),' he says, 'and are cast out (ἐκβάλλω) into the drain (ἀφεδρών),' while the things going out of the mouth are evil 'thoughts' spoken (λαλέω) and 'murders' (φόνοι) and 'adulteries' (μοιχεῖαι) and 'fornications (πορνεῖαι), thefts (κλοπαί)' and 'false witnessings' and 'blasphemies' (βλασφημίαι). And Paul too says that 'food will not present (παρίστημι) us to God; for neither if we eat do we abound (περισσεύω), nor if we do not eat do we lack (ὑστερέω).' Then, since these have some obscurity (ἀσάφεια) unless they meet with articulation/clarification (διάρθρωσις), 'it seemed good (δοκέω) to the apostles' of Jesus 'and to the elders (πρεσβύτεροι)' gathered together (συνάγω) in Antioch, and, as these themselves named, also 'to the Holy Spirit (ἅγιον πνεῦμα)' to write to those believing from the nations (ἔθνη) a letter (ἐπιστολή) forbidding (ἀπαγορεύω) to eat only the things, as they named, 'necessary' (ἐπάναγκες); and these are either things sacrificed to idols (εἰδωλόθυτα) or things strangled (πνικτά) or blood.
pass_b_english: It should be understood, however, that while the Jews think they understand the law of Moses, and in the matter of foods keep the rule of eating what they hold to be clean and abstaining from what is unclean, and also of not using an animal’s blood for food, nor what has been torn by wild beasts, and other such things (there is much to say about these, and for that reason this is not the right time to examine them), the teaching of Jesus wished to call all men to the pure worship of God, and not, on the pretext of a heavier law about foods, to hinder many of those whose character could be helped by Christianity. So it declared: “It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matthew 15:11). For what “goes into the mouth,” he says, “passes into the stomach and is cast out into the drain” (Matthew 15:17); but what comes out of the mouth are “evil thoughts” put into words, and “murders,” “adulteries,” “fornications,” “thefts,” “false witness,” and “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19).

Paul too says: “Food will not commend us to God; for if we eat, we are no better off, and if we do not eat, we are no worse off” (1 Corinthians 8:8). Then, since these words have a certain obscurity unless they are spelled out, “it seemed good to the apostles” of Jesus “and to the elders” who had gathered together at Antioch, and, as they themselves put it, “to the Holy Spirit,” to write a letter to the believers from among the Gentiles (Acts 15:22–23, 28). The only foods this letter forbade them to eat were those which, as they put it, were “necessary”: that is, things offered to idols, or things strangled, or blood (Acts 15:28–29).

choices.choice: The saying of Jesus follows Matthew’s form (κοινοῖ, ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται); the parallel is Mark 7:15, 18-21. Origen adds ‘spoken’ (λαλούμενοι) to ‘evil thoughts’ as his own gloss; I kept it as ‘put into words’, outside the quotation marks. 1 Corinthians 8:8: περισσεύομεν/ὑστερούμεθα rendered ‘better off’/’worse off’; Origen gives the two clauses in the reverse order from Paul, and his order is kept. Origen says the apostles and elders were gathered ‘at Antioch’; in Acts 15 the council meets in Jerusalem and the letter is sent to Antioch. I translated the Greek as it stands and did not correct it. The decree in Acts 15:29 also names fornication; Origen lists only the food items, since foods are his subject. ‘Things torn by wild beasts’ (θηριάλωτα) recalls Exodus 22:31 and Leviticus 17:15; uncited inline because it is a summary of the law rather than a quotation. The opening sentence keeps the Greek structure: the Jews’ practice is a ‘while’ clause (genitive absolute) and ‘the teaching of Jesus’ is the main subject.
first sentence restructured so 'It should be understood' governs the main point (the teaching of Jesus), with the Jews' practice as a 'while' clause, as in the Greek genitive absolute
'caught by wild beasts' changed to 'torn by wild beasts' (θηριάλωτα, the usual English for the Mosaic category)
ambiguous 'forbade them to eat only those things' recast as 'The only foods this letter forbade them to eat were those ...'
translator note: recorded Origen's reversed clause order in 1 Corinthians 8:8 and the sentence structure

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
